knowledge_point.title: Finding an Area by Transforming to a Type I Region

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x - 8 y,\,v=y + 3,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(x - 8 y)^{2}+y=5$ and the line $y=0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x - 8 y,\,v=y + 3
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Substituting $x - 8 y=u$ and $y + 3=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
(x - 8 y)^{2}+y=5\,⟹\,(y+3)=8-(x - 8 y)^{2}\,⟹\,v=8 - u^{2}.
$$

while substituting $y + 3=v$ into the equation of the line, we obtain

$$
v=3.
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}v=3 \\ v=8 - u^{2}\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,u=\pm \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt{5},3).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,- \sqrt{5}\le u\le \sqrt{5},\,3\le v\le 8 - u^{2}\}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/repairs/2026-10-20-early-cohort/jobs/17592186129197/review-1-policy-2-6d8162cdaa407593/runtime/plots/4726d6e82047119ff4c582e6.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\left|\begin{matrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{matrix}\right| \\ &=\left|\begin{matrix}1&-8\\0&1\end{matrix}\right| \\ &=1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D dxdy &=\iint_Δ |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,dudv \\ &=\iint_Δ |1|\,dudv \\ &=1\int_{- \sqrt{5}}^{\sqrt{5}}[\int_{3}^{8 - u^{2}}dv]du \\ &=1\int_{- \sqrt{5}}^{\sqrt{5}}[v]_{3}^{8 - u^{2}}du \\ &=1\int_{- \sqrt{5}}^{\sqrt{5}}(8 - u^{2})-(3)du \\ &=1\int_{- \sqrt{5}}^{\sqrt{5}}(5 - u^{2})du \\ &=1[- \frac{u^{3}}{3} + 5 u]_{- \sqrt{5}}^{\sqrt{5}} \\ &=1(((5 \sqrt{5})+(- \frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{3}))-((- 5 \sqrt{5})+(\frac{5 \sqrt{5}}{3}))) \\ &=1(\frac{20 \sqrt{5}}{3}) \\ &=\frac{20 \sqrt{5}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
(x - 8 y)^{2}-(y)=-4\,⟹\,u^{2}-v=-4\,⟹\,v=u^{2} + 4.
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
v=7.
$$

$$

$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt{3},7).$

Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,- \sqrt{3}\le u\le \sqrt{3},\,u^{2} + 4\le v\le 7\}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/repairs/2026-10-20-early-cohort/jobs/17592186129197/review-1-policy-2-6d8162cdaa407593/runtime/plots/4dda8676208119a226e42c67.png)

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\left|\begin{matrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{matrix}\right| \\ &=\left|\begin{matrix}1&-8\\0&1\end{matrix}\right| \\ &=1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D dxdy &=\iint_Δ |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,dudv \\ &=\iint_Δ |1|\,dudv \\ &=1\int_{- \sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}}[\int_{u^{2} + 4}^{7}dv]du \\ &=1\int_{- \sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}}[v]_{u^{2} + 4}^{7}du \\ &=1\int_{- \sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}}(7)-(u^{2} + 4)du \\ &=1\int_{- \sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}}(3 - u^{2})du \\ &=1[- \frac{u^{3}}{3} + 3 u]_{- \sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}} \\ &=1(((3 \sqrt{3})+(- \sqrt{3}))-((- 3 \sqrt{3})+(\sqrt{3}))) \\ &=1(4 \sqrt{3}) \\ &=4 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem:
Using the change of variables 

$$
u=x - 8 y,\,v=x + 8 y,
$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the lines $x + 8 y=1,$ $x - 8 y=1$ and the curve $x^{2} - 64 y^{2}=10.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x - 8 y,\,v=x + 8 y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

Substituting $x + 8 y=v$ into the equation of the first line, we get

$$
x + 8 y=1\,⟹\,v=1.
$$

while substituting $x - 8 y=u$ into the equation of the second line, we obtain

$$
x - 8 y=1\,⟹\,u=1.
$$

Substituting $x + 8 y=v$ and $x - 8 y=u$ into the equation of curve, we get

$$
x^{2} - 64 y^{2}=10\,⟹\,(x - 8 y)(x + 8 y)=10\,⟹\,uv=10.
$$

The intersection point of the two lines in the $uv$-plane is $(1,1).$

To find the intersection of the curve with the first line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}uv=10 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}v=1 \\ u=10\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curve with the second line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}uv=10 \\ u=1\end{aligned}\right.\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}u=1 \\ v=10\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(1,1),$ $(1,10)$ and $(10,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 10,\,1\le v\le \frac{10}{u}\}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/repairs/2026-10-20-early-cohort/jobs/17592186129197/review-1-policy-2-6d8162cdaa407593/runtime/plots/0775ec30584962f7661d5bb4.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =\left|\begin{matrix}\frac{∂u}{∂x}&\frac{∂u}{∂y}\\\frac{∂v}{∂x}&\frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{matrix}\right| \\ &=\left|\begin{matrix}1&-8\\1&8\end{matrix}\right| \\ &=16\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(16)^{-1}=\frac{1}{16}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D dxdy &=\iint_Δ |\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,dudv \\ &=\iint_Δ |\frac{1}{16}|\,dudv \\ &=\frac{1}{16}\int_{1}^{10}[\int_{1}^{\frac{10}{u}}dv]du \\ &=\frac{1}{16}\int_{1}^{10}[v]_{1}^{\frac{10}{u}}du \\ &=\frac{1}{16}\int_{1}^{10}(\frac{10}{u})-(1)du \\ &=\frac{1}{16}[- u + 10 \ln{\left(u \right)}]_{1}^{10} \\ &=\frac{1}{16}(((10 \ln{\left(10 \right)})+(-10))-((0)+(-1))) \\ &=\frac{1}{16}(-9 + \ln{\left(10000000000 \right)}) \\ &=- \frac{9}{16} + \frac{5 \ln{\left(10 \right)}}{8}\end{aligned}
$$
